analysis.one_liner: Caps power plant carbon emissions and lets utilities trade pollution allowances, with auction money funding clean energy and worker aid.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on January 17, 2007, received no committee action or floor vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5][S1].
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a yearly ceiling on carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted by large electric power plants, starting in 2011 at 2006 levels and shrinking about 1% each year through 2019 and 1.5% each year after that. Power plants would have complied by buying and selling pollution allowances; the share given away free to existing plants would start at 85% and shrink to zero by 2036, while auctioned allowances would fund clean energy technology, help for low-income energy consumers and displaced workers, and wildlife habitat programs. Farmers and foresters could have earned credits for practices that store carbon. The bill never got beyond its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to climate change benefits from an enforceable cap on power sector emissions, which are among the largest sources of U.S. carbon pollution [S2][S3]. The bill also directs at least 10% of auction revenue to assistance for low-income energy consumers facing higher bills, displaced workers, and hard-hit communities, and creates new revenue opportunities for farmers, foresters, and landowners through offset credits [S3]. Nuclear and renewable generators gain commercially: incremental nuclear output counts toward valuable allowances and new renewable units receive allocations [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, workers, farmers, and clean energy

how_it_helps.text: Beginning in 2011 the bill would cap total greenhouse gas emissions from power plants over 25 megawatts at 2006 levels, then reduce the cap 1% annually through 2019 and 1.5% annually from 2020 onward, with mandatory EPA review of whether deeper cuts are needed to reach a 'safe climate level' [S2][S3].

Auction proceeds go into a Climate Action Trust Fund that must spend at least 10% on adaptation help for workers and communities, including low-income energy consumers facing higher bills, and at least 10% on protecting fish and wildlife habitat from climate impacts [S3].
The fund would also finance programs for low- and zero-carbon generation technologies, clean coal technology, and energy efficiency in buildings and industry [S2][S3].

Agricultural producers, foresters, and other landowners could earn offset credits for practices like no-till farming, cover cropping, and forest management, with USDA outreach to help them market those credits for new revenue [S2][S3].
Exceeding the cap carries penalties of 1.3 credits per excess ton plus a cash penalty per ton, and every allowance can be terminated or limited by the EPA, giving the cap real teeth [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities bear the cost of the cap, and they can pass much of it to households and businesses through electricity rates, especially as the free-allowance share shrinks. The coal industry loses demand as plants face a shrinking ceiling, and new coal plants are denied free allowances unless they use qualifying advanced clean coal technology [S3].

drawbacks.text: 85% of allowances would initially be given free to existing power plants, handing generators valuable assets rather than raising public revenue, and ratepayers would still face the opportunity cost of those allowances in their electricity prices [S3].

Utilities could meet up to 25% of their obligation with international credits, up to 50% for new units, and the EPA could raise that to 50% and allow borrowing against future allowances if allowance prices were deemed to be harming the economy, escape valves that could slow emission cuts [S3].
The cap covers only the electric power sector, not transportation or industry, so economy-wide emissions would continue elsewhere [S2][S3].
Offset credits from farming and forestry are difficult to measure and verify, and poorly policed offsets can credit changes that would have happened anyway, undermining the cap [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has a real, enforceable downward trajectory for power sector carbon and directs revenue to the people most exposed to both climate damage and higher energy prices. Its weaknesses are the slow start (emissions frozen at 2006 levels through 2014), the large free allowance allocation to incumbents, and the economic-harm escape valve, all of which reduce near-term cuts and raise the chance that costs land on ratepayers before the auction share grows. On balance it is a genuine climate program with incumbent-friendly design features, not a giveaway bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in January 2007, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein, for herself and Sen. Thomas Carper, introduced the Electric Utility Cap and Trade Act on January 17, 2007; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S3][S5].

The bill's only cosponsor was a single Democrat, and no committee markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind appears in its action history before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S4][S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil-fueled power generators were better off: they faced no federal carbon cap for the rest of the Congress and kept emitting without compliance costs. Farmers, low-income energy consumers, and displaced workers never received the assistance and offset revenue the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil power generators avoided carbon limits

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on January 17, 2007.

for.name: Sen. Thomas Carper
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Barbara Boxer (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on S. 317; the committee's major climate effort that Congress was the separate Lieberman-Warner cap-and-trade bill, which also died.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split is recorded; both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, though Carper was known for bipartisan climate work.

industries.note: They would bear the cost of a shrinking emissions cap but receive 85% of allowances free at the start, a large asset that declines to zero by 2036. Their interest in avoiding or softening the cap runs against the public's interest in emission reductions, and allowance costs ultimately flow into electricity rates.

industries.industry: Coal producers and new coal plant developers
industries.note: New coal-fired units get no free allowances unless they use qualifying advanced clean coal technology, and the overall cap shrinks coal demand over time. A clean coal technology program funded by the auction proceeds is the offsetting carve-out.

Incremental nuclear generation counts toward allowance allocations, renewable units receive allocations, and the fund finances low- and zero-carbon technology deployment, all of which raise the value of non-fossil generation.

Offset credits for practices like no-till farming, cover cropping, grazing and forest management would create a new revenue stream, with USDA running an outreach program to help landowners market credits.
